case: A 58-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her husband because of a 1-year history of apathy and loss of interest in her usual activities and a 6-month history of daily dull headaches. She says she has not been able to smell coffee or perfume for about 2 years. Physical examination shows she cannot identify coffee or peppermint by smell with either nostril. Funduscopic examination shows optic atrophy on the right and papilledema on the left. Strength, sensation, and reflexes are normal. MRI of the brain shows a 5-cm homogeneously enhancing extra-axial mass with a dural tail arising from the floor of the anterior cranial fossa over the cribriform plate and compressing both frontal lobes. Diagnosis: olfactory groove meningioma.

questions.stem: The mass is resected. Which of the following is most likely to be found on microscopic examination of the tumor?
options: Pseudopalisading tumor cells around necrosis
Round cells with perinuclear halos and branching capillaries
Whorled clusters of cells with psammoma bodies
Small blue cells forming Homer Wright rosettes
approach: Note the clues for an extra-axial tumor: attached to the dura, with a dural tail, pushing on the brain from outside.
A dural-based tumor in an adult woman is a meningioma, which arises from arachnoid cap cells.
Recall its histology: whorls of meningothelial cells and laminated calcifications called psammoma bodies.
questions.why: Meningioma is a usually benign tumor of arachnoid cap (meningothelial) cells. It sits outside the brain, attaches to the dura, and often shows a dural tail on MRI. Under the microscope the cells form whorls, and some whorls calcify into layered psammoma bodies. It is more common in women and is linked to NF2 and prior head radiation. Symptoms come from compression; here the frontal lobes cause apathy, and the olfactory bulbs and optic nerve explain the anosmia and the eye findings.
whyNot: Pseudopalisading necrosis is the mark of glioblastoma, an intra-axial tumor of the cerebral white matter that often crosses the corpus callosum.
Perinuclear halos (fried egg cells) with branching chicken-wire capillaries describe oligodendroglioma, an intra-axial frontal lobe tumor that often calcifies and causes seizures.
Correct.
Homer Wright rosettes of small blue cells are seen in medulloblastoma, a cerebellar tumor of children, and in neuroblastoma.

questions.stem: Her loss of smell results from compression of the olfactory bulbs and tracts. Which of the following best describes the normal central pathway of this sensation?
options: Olfactory tract fibers reach the piriform cortex without a thalamic relay
Olfactory nerve fibers relay in the nucleus solitarius before reaching cortex
Olfactory tract fibers relay in the VPM nucleus before reaching insular cortex
Olfactory tract fibers relay in the medial geniculate nucleus before reaching cortex
approach: Trace smell from the receptor: olfactory neurons pass through the cribriform plate and synapse in the olfactory bulb.
Recall that the olfactory tract projects straight to primary olfactory (piriform) cortex and the amygdala.
Smell is the one sense that reaches cortex without first relaying in the thalamus.
questions.why: Olfactory receptor neurons in the nasal roof send their axons (CN I) through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to synapse on mitral cells in the olfactory bulb. The olfactory tract then runs back under the frontal lobe to the piriform cortex and amygdala in the medial temporal lobe, with no thalamic relay. An olfactory groove mass presses on the bulbs and tracts from below. A fracture of the cribriform plate tears the olfactory nerve fibers and causes anosmia, often with CSF rhinorrhea.
whyNot: Correct.
The nucleus solitarius receives taste from CN VII, IX, and X and visceral input from CN IX and X. It plays no part in smell.
VPM relays face sensation and taste to cortex. Taste reaches the insula and frontal operculum this way, but smell does not use VPM.
The medial geniculate nucleus relays hearing to the primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe.

questions.stem: Her 31-year-old daughter has had recurrent episodes of throbbing left-sided headache since adolescence. Each episode lasts about 12 hours, brings nausea and sensitivity to light and sound, and follows 20 minutes of flickering zigzag lines in her vision. Neurologic examination between episodes is normal. Which of the following mechanisms most directly produces the daughter's headache pain?
options: Sustained contraction and tenderness of pericranial muscles
Hypothalamic activation driving a trigeminal autonomic reflex
Impaired CSF absorption raising intracranial pressure
Trigeminovascular activation with release of CGRP
approach: Classify the headache: unilateral, pulsating, hours long, with nausea, photophobia, phonophobia, and a visual aura. This is migraine with aura.
Recall the pain mechanism of migraine: trigeminal sensory fibers around meningeal vessels release CGRP and other peptides.
Match the other mechanisms to tension headache, cluster headache, and raised intracranial pressure.
questions.why: Migraine is a recurrent unilateral pulsating headache lasting about 4 to 72 hours, with nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia. About a third of patients have an aura, often spreading visual zigzags, which reflects a wave of cortical spreading depression. The pain comes from activation of the trigeminovascular system: trigeminal afferents around dural and pial vessels release calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), which dilates vessels and causes neurogenic inflammation and sensitization. This is why drugs that block CGRP prevent migraine.
whyNot: Pericranial muscle tenderness goes with tension-type headache, a bilateral band-like pressure without nausea, aura, or marked photophobia.
Hypothalamic activation with a trigeminal autonomic reflex underlies cluster headache: brief (15 to 180 minutes) severe periorbital pain with same-side tearing and rhinorrhea, often in men.

Raised intracranial pressure, as with her mother's mass or idiopathic intracranial hypertension, causes daily headache worse lying down, often with papilledema. Her headaches are episodic with a normal examination between attacks.
Correct.

questions.stem: Eight months after surgery, she slips on ice and strikes the side of her head. She is unconscious for a minute, then talks normally for 2 hours before becoming drowsy. CT scan of the head shows a biconvex hyperdense collection over the left temporal lobe that does not cross suture lines, beneath a fracture of the squamous temporal bone. This blood has most likely collected in which of the following spaces?
options: Between the dura and the arachnoid mater
Between the skull and the dura mater
Between the arachnoid and the pia mater
Within the parenchyma of the temporal lobe
approach: Read the clues: temporal bone fracture, lucid interval, and a biconvex collection stopped by suture lines.
This is an epidural hematoma from a torn middle meningeal artery.
Arterial blood strips the dura off the skull, so it collects between the inner table of the skull and the dura.
questions.why: The middle meningeal artery runs in a groove on the inner surface of the squamous temporal bone near the pterion, where the bone is thin. A fracture here can tear it, and arterial pressure peels the dura away from the skull. The dura is firmly fixed at the sutures, so the blood forms a lens-shaped (biconvex) collection that stops at suture lines. The classic course is brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval, then rapid decline as the hematoma expands.
whyNot: Blood between the dura and arachnoid is a subdural hematoma from torn bridging veins. It is crescent-shaped, crosses suture lines, and is common in older adults and people with alcohol use disorder.
Correct.
Blood between the arachnoid and pia is subarachnoid hemorrhage, most often from a ruptured berry aneurysm, with sudden thunderclap headache and blood in the basal cisterns.
Bleeding into the temporal lobe itself would be a contusion or intraparenchymal hemorrhage, seen inside the brain rather than as a lens-shaped collection under the skull.

case: A 23-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of progressive hearing loss in both ears, constant ringing in his ears, and unsteadiness when walking in the dark. He had surgery for a cataract in his left eye at age 17 years. Physical examination shows decreased hearing to whispered voice bilaterally. On Rinne testing, air conduction is greater than bone conduction in both ears. He sways when standing with his eyes closed. Facial sensation and facial movement are normal. MRI of the brain with contrast shows bilateral enhancing masses at the cerebellopontine angles that extend into the internal acoustic canals, and a small dural-based mass over the right frontal convexity. Diagnosis: bilateral vestibular schwannomas in neurofibromatosis type 2.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the site where these tumors most likely originate?
options: Vestibular nuclei at the pontomedullary junction of the brainstem
Vestibular nerve within the internal acoustic canal
Spiral ganglion in the modiolus of the cochlea
Facial nerve at the geniculate ganglion
approach: A schwannoma is a tumor of Schwann cells, so it must arise where a nerve has peripheral myelin.
CN VIII is myelinated by oligodendrocytes near the brainstem and by Schwann cells farther out, with the transition near the internal acoustic canal.
Hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance with masses at the cerebellopontine angle point to the vestibular division of CN VIII.
questions.why: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) almost always arises from the vestibular division of CN VIII, near the junction of central and peripheral myelin within the internal acoustic canal. As it grows, it fills the canal and pushes into the cerebellopontine angle. It compresses the cochlear nerve (hearing loss and tinnitus) and the vestibular nerve (imbalance), and large tumors later press on CN V (facial numbness, lost corneal reflex) and CN VII. Under the microscope it shows S-100 positive Schwann cells in dense Antoni A areas with Verocay bodies and loose Antoni B areas. Bilateral tumors define NF2.
whyNot: The vestibular nuclei are CNS neurons inside the brainstem. There are no Schwann cells there, and a tumor there would be intra-axial.
Correct.
The spiral ganglion holds cochlear neuron cell bodies inside the cochlea. A lesion here could cause hearing loss but would not form an enhancing mass at the cerebellopontine angle.
Facial nerve schwannomas are rare and usually present with facial weakness. His facial movement is normal.

questions.stem: Molecular analysis of the resected tumor shows loss of both copies of the gene that causes his disorder. The normal product of this gene most likely functions as which of the following?
options: A GTPase-activating protein that turns off Ras signaling
A ubiquitin ligase subunit that targets HIF-1 alpha for breakdown
A Rheb GTPase-activating protein that restrains mTOR activity
A cytoskeletal scaffold protein that mediates contact inhibition
approach: Name the disorder: bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningioma, and juvenile cataract mean NF2.
Recall the NF2 gene on chromosome 22, which encodes the tumor suppressor merlin (schwannomin).
Merlin links membrane proteins to the actin cytoskeleton and stops growth when cells touch.
questions.why: NF2 is caused by loss of the NF2 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 22. Its product, merlin, is a cytoskeletal scaffold related to the ERM proteins. It links cell membrane receptors to actin and mediates contact inhibition, so its loss lets Schwann cells and meningothelial cells keep dividing. Like other tumor suppressor syndromes, NF2 is inherited as autosomal dominant, but a tumor forms only after the second allele is lost in a cell (two-hit model). About half of cases are new mutations.
whyNot: This is neurofibromin, the NF1 gene product on chromosome 17. Its loss leaves Ras active and causes neurofibromas and café-au-lait macules.
This is the VHL protein, encoded on chromosome 3. Its loss stabilizes HIF and causes hemangioblastomas and renal cell carcinoma.
This is tuberin (TSC2), which partners with hamartin (TSC1). Their loss activates mTOR and causes tuberous sclerosis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Another patient, an 8-year-old girl, has six café-au-lait macules larger than 5 mm, freckling in both axillae, and pigmented iris hamartomas on slit-lamp examination. She is at greatest risk for which of the following tumors?
options: Optic pathway glioma
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas
Cerebellar hemangioblastoma
Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma
approach: Identify the syndrome: multiple café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, and Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas) define NF1.
Recall the CNS tumor most typical of NF1 in children: a low-grade pilocytic glioma of the optic nerve or chiasm.
Assign the other tumors to NF2, von Hippel-Lindau disease, and tuberous sclerosis.
questions.why: Neurofibromatosis type 1 shows café-au-lait macules, axillary or inguinal freckling, cutaneous neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules. Optic pathway glioma, usually a pilocytic astrocytoma, is the most common CNS tumor in children with NF1 and can cause vision loss or precocious puberty. Plexiform neurofibromas can turn into malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors, and adults have a higher risk of pheochromocytoma. NF1 comes from loss of neurofibromin on chromosome 17.
whyNot: Correct.
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas define NF2, which has few skin findings and no Lisch nodules.
Cerebellar hemangioblastoma is the typical CNS tumor of von Hippel-Lindau disease.
Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma near the foramen of Monro is a feature of tuberous sclerosis, which has ash-leaf spots rather than café-au-lait macules.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has a cerebellar hemangioblastoma and two retinal hemangioblastomas. Genetic testing shows a germline loss-of-function mutation on chromosome 3p in a gene whose product targets hypoxia-inducible factor for degradation. She is at greatest risk for which of the following additional tumors?
options: Cardiac rhabdomyoma
Renal angiomyolipoma
Clear cell renal cell carcinoma
Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor
approach: Cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas with a chromosome 3p mutation identify von Hippel-Lindau disease.
Without VHL protein, HIF is not degraded, so cells keep making VEGF and other hypoxia genes, which drives vascular tumors.
The main malignant risk in this disease is clear cell renal cell carcinoma, often bilateral.
questions.why: The VHL protein is part of a ubiquitin ligase that tags hypoxia-inducible factor for breakdown when oxygen is normal. When both copies are lost, HIF builds up and switches on VEGF, PDGF, and erythropoietin genes as if the cell were hypoxic. The result is highly vascular tumors: hemangioblastomas of the cerebellum, spinal cord, and retina; clear cell renal cell carcinoma, often multiple and bilateral; pheochromocytoma; and pancreatic cysts. Renal cell carcinoma is a leading cause of death in this disease.
whyNot: Cardiac rhabdomyoma is a tumor of tuberous sclerosis, along with cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, and ash-leaf spots.
Renal angiomyolipoma is also a feature of tuberous sclerosis, caused by TSC1 or TSC2 loss with mTOR activation.
Correct.
Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor arises from plexiform neurofibromas in NF1.

dx: Pituitary macroadenoma compressing the optic chiasm
case: A 47-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of headaches and repeatedly bumping into door frames on both sides. He has had decreased libido and erectile dysfunction for 1 year. Visual field testing shows loss of the temporal half of the visual field in each eye. Visual acuity and pupillary light reflexes are normal. Serum LH and testosterone concentrations are decreased. MRI of the head shows a 2.8-cm sellar mass with suprasellar extension that elevates and compresses the optic chiasm and displaces the pituitary stalk. Diagnosis: nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma compressing the optic chiasm.

questions.stem: Serum prolactin concentration is 58 ng/mL (N, 2 to 18 ng/mL). After transsphenoidal resection, immunohistochemical staining of the tumor is negative for prolactin and all other pituitary hormones. Which of the following best explains his increased serum prolactin?
options: Interrupted dopamine delivery from the hypothalamus
Prolactin secretion by a subset of tumor cells
Increased TRH release from compressed hypothalamic neurons
Release of stored prolactin from the posterior pituitary
approach: Recall that prolactin is the one anterior pituitary hormone held down mainly by hypothalamic inhibition, through dopamine.
Dopamine from the arcuate nucleus reaches lactotrophs through the portal vessels in the pituitary stalk.
A mass that compresses the stalk cuts off dopamine, so normal lactotrophs release more prolactin (stalk effect).
questions.why: Dopamine made in the arcuate nucleus travels down the tuberoinfundibular tract and through the hypophyseal portal vessels of the stalk to inhibit lactotrophs. When a sellar mass compresses the stalk, this brake is lost and normal lactotrophs raise prolactin modestly, usually below about 100 to 150 ng/mL. A prolactin-secreting macroadenoma usually produces much higher levels. Telling the two apart matters because a prolactinoma shrinks with dopamine agonists, while a nonfunctioning adenoma does not. The same mass explains his bitemporal hemianopia, since it presses on the crossing nasal retinal fibers in the chiasm.
whyNot: Correct.
The tumor stains negative for prolactin, so the adenoma cells are not the source.
TRH can stimulate prolactin release, but a sellar mass interferes with hypothalamic signals reaching the pituitary rather than increasing them.
The posterior pituitary stores ADH and oxytocin only. Prolactin is made and released by lactotrophs of the anterior pituitary.

questions.stem: On the second day after surgery, he passes 6 L of dilute urine. Serum sodium concentration is 149 mEq/L (N, 135 to 145 mEq/L), plasma osmolality is 305 mOsm/kg H2O (N, 275 to 295 mOsm/kg H2O), and urine osmolality is 110 mOsm/kg H2O. Which of the following most likely accounts for these findings?
options: Resistance of collecting duct principal cells to ADH
Loss of ACTH secretion from anterior pituitary corticotrophs
Injured supraoptic and paraventricular axons in the stalk
Excess thirst with suppression of ADH secretion
approach: Interpret the labs: large volumes of dilute urine while plasma is concentrated and sodium is high means too little ADH effect.
Recall where ADH comes from: supraoptic and paraventricular neurons send axons down the stalk to the posterior pituitary.
Surgery around the stalk injures these axons, causing central diabetes insipidus.
questions.why: ADH (vasopressin) and oxytocin are made in the cell bodies of supraoptic and paraventricular neurons, carried down their axons through the pituitary stalk, and stored in the posterior pituitary. Pituitary surgery or head trauma can injure these axons, so ADH release falls and the collecting ducts cannot reabsorb water. Urine becomes large in volume and dilute while plasma osmolality and sodium rise. Urine concentrates after desmopressin, which confirms a central cause. After surgery this can be transient or follow a triphasic course of diabetes insipidus, then SIADH as damaged terminals leak stored ADH, then permanent diabetes insipidus.
whyNot: Collecting duct resistance to ADH is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, caused by lithium, hypercalcemia, or receptor mutations. It would not start suddenly after pituitary surgery and would not respond to desmopressin.
Cortisol deficiency from lost ACTH impairs free water excretion and tends to cause hyponatremia, the opposite of his findings.
Correct.
Primary polydipsia also gives dilute urine, but drinking too much water lowers plasma osmolality and sodium. His are high.

questions.stem: The suprasellar part of the tumor reaches the floor of the third ventricle. A hypothalamic nucleus that lies just above the optic chiasm receives direct input from retinal ganglion cells. Damage to this nucleus would most likely disrupt which of the following functions?
options: Satiety signaling after a meal
Circadian sleep-wake rhythm
Heat loss through sweating and vasodilation
Oxytocin release during lactation
approach: Identify the nucleus: the suprachiasmatic nucleus sits above the optic chiasm and receives the retinohypothalamic tract.
Recall its job: it is the master clock that sets circadian rhythms to the light-dark cycle.
Assign the other functions to the ventromedial, anterior, and paraventricular nuclei.
questions.why: The suprachiasmatic nucleus receives light information directly from a small group of retinal ganglion cells through the retinohypothalamic tract. It sets the timing of sleep and wakefulness, body temperature cycles, and hormone rhythms such as cortisol and melatonin. It controls melatonin release from the pineal gland through a pathway that runs through the sympathetic system. Damage disrupts the daily sleep-wake cycle.
whyNot: Satiety depends on the ventromedial nucleus. A lesion there causes hyperphagia and obesity.
Correct.
Heat loss is run by the anterior hypothalamus (preoptic area). A lesion there causes hyperthermia.
Oxytocin is made in the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei and released from the posterior pituitary.

questions.stem: Most of the axons compressed by this tumor normally make their next synapse in which of the following structures?
options: Medial geniculate nucleus
Ventral posterolateral nucleus
Ventral posteromedial nucleus
Lateral geniculate nucleus
approach: The tumor compresses the optic chiasm, which carries retinal ganglion cell axons.
These axons continue in the optic tract and most of them synapse in the thalamus.
The thalamic relay for vision is the lateral geniculate nucleus, which sends the optic radiations to visual cortex.
questions.why: Retinal ganglion cell axons from both eyes meet in the optic chiasm, where nasal fibers cross. They continue in the optic tracts, and most synapse in the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, which projects through the optic radiations to the primary visual cortex. Each sensory system has its own thalamic relay: VPL for body sensation, VPM for face sensation and taste, LGN for vision, and MGN for hearing, with VL relaying motor signals. A thalamic infarct causes contralateral sensory loss and can later cause thalamic pain syndrome.
whyNot: The medial geniculate nucleus relays hearing from the inferior colliculus to auditory cortex.
VPL relays touch, vibration, pain, and temperature from the body through the medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tract.
VPM relays sensation from the face through the trigeminal pathways and taste from the nucleus solitarius.
Correct.

case: A 19-year-old college student who lives in a dormitory is brought to the emergency department 10 hours after the onset of fever, severe headache, and vomiting. His temperature is 39.8 °C (103.6 °F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. He is drowsy and has neck stiffness and photophobia. Nonblanching petechiae are present on his legs and trunk. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 32 cm H2O (N, 10 to 20 cm H2O). CSF analysis shows leukocytes 2,800/µL (N, 0 to 5/µL) with 90% neutrophils, glucose 18 mg/dL (N, 40 to 70 mg/dL), and protein 260 mg/dL (N, 15 to 45 mg/dL). Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci. Diagnosis: meningococcal meningitis.

questions.stem: Over the next 6 hours, the petechiae enlarge into purpura, and his blood pressure falls to 78/40 mm Hg. Which of the following bacterial components most directly triggers these changes?
options: Pneumolysin
Polyribosylribitol phosphate capsule
Lipoteichoic acid
Lipooligosaccharide
approach: Gram-negative diplococci in CSF with a petechial rash identify Neisseria meningitidis.
Purpura with falling blood pressure means septic shock with disseminated intravascular coagulation.
The outer membrane endotoxin of N. meningitidis, lipooligosaccharide, drives this cytokine storm.
questions.why: Neisseria meningitidis is a gram-negative diplococcus with two key virulence factors. Its polysaccharide capsule protects it from phagocytosis and complement. Its outer membrane lipooligosaccharide (LOS) is an endotoxin that it sheds in large amounts in membrane blebs. Lipid A binds TLR4 on macrophages and endothelium and triggers TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 release, endothelial damage, DIC, and shock. Severe cases can cause adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome).
whyNot: Pneumolysin is a pore-forming toxin of Streptococcus pneumoniae, a gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococcus.
Polyribosylribitol phosphate is the capsule of Haemophilus influenzae type b, a gram-negative coccobacillus. Capsules block phagocytosis but do not directly cause shock.
Lipoteichoic acid is a cell wall component of gram-positive bacteria. N. meningitidis is gram-negative.
Correct.

questions.stem: His roommate received a meningococcal conjugate vaccine at age 16 years. In this vaccine, the capsular polysaccharide is linked to a protein carrier. Which of the following best explains why conjugation improves protection compared with plain polysaccharide?
options: It allows the polysaccharide to activate CD8 cytotoxic T cells
It recruits helper T cells, giving class switching and memory
It makes the polysaccharide a ligand for Toll-like receptor 4
It lets the polysaccharide cross-link B cell receptors
approach: Recall that plain polysaccharide antigens activate B cells without T cell help, giving mostly IgM and little memory.
T cells recognize only peptides on MHC. Linking a protein carrier to the polysaccharide supplies those peptides.
The B cell that binds the polysaccharide presents carrier peptides on MHC class II and gets help from CD4 T cells.
questions.why: A B cell whose receptor binds the capsular polysaccharide takes in the whole conjugate, breaks down the protein carrier, and presents its peptides on MHC class II. Carrier-specific CD4 helper T cells then give CD40 ligand and cytokine signals to that B cell. This produces class switching to IgG, affinity maturation, and long-lived memory B cells against the polysaccharide. Conjugate vaccines also work in infants under 2 years, who respond poorly to plain polysaccharide. The same principle is used for H. influenzae type b and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines.
whyNot: CD8 T cells recognize peptides on MHC class I. Polysaccharides are not presented to CD8 T cells, and protection against capsule depends on antibody.
Correct.
TLR4 recognizes lipid A of endotoxin. Conjugation to a protein does not turn polysaccharide into a TLR4 ligand.
Plain polysaccharide already cross-links B cell receptors through its repeating units. That is how it causes a T cell-independent IgM response without memory.

topics: T cell-dependent and T cell-independent antigens

questions.stem: His 52-year-old uncle, who recently moved from a country where tuberculosis is endemic, develops 4 weeks of low-grade fever, headache, and confusion, followed by double vision from a right abducens nerve palsy. CSF shows 220 leukocytes/µL, mostly lymphocytes, glucose 22 mg/dL, and protein 310 mg/dL. Which of the following is most likely to be found in the uncle's brain?
options: Purulent neutrophilic exudate over the cerebral convexities
Hemorrhagic necrosis of the medial temporal lobes
Thick gelatinous basal exudate with caseating granulomas
Spongiform vacuoles without inflammatory cells
approach: Note the subacute course over weeks, a cranial nerve palsy, and CSF with lymphocytes, very low glucose, and very high protein.
This pattern in a person from an endemic area is tuberculous meningitis.
Recall its pathology: a thick exudate at the base of the brain with granulomas that traps cranial nerves and vessels.
questions.why: Tuberculous meningitis develops over weeks. Mycobacterium tuberculosis seeds the meninges, and a thick gelatinous exudate with caseating granulomas collects around the base of the brain. It traps cranial nerves (CN VI, with its long course, and CN III and IV), inflames basal arteries and causes infarcts, and blocks CSF flow at the basal cisterns, causing hydrocephalus. CSF shows lymphocytes, very low glucose, and very high protein. Acute bacterial meningitis like the student's has other complications too: sensorineural hearing loss, seizures, and hydrocephalus.
whyNot: A purulent exudate over the convexities fits acute pyogenic meningitis, such as pneumococcal meningitis, with neutrophils in CSF and a course of hours to days.
Hemorrhagic necrosis of the temporal lobes is the pattern of herpes simplex encephalitis, with confusion, seizures, and a lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose.
Correct.
Spongiform change without inflammation marks prion disease, a rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus and no fever or CSF pleocytosis.

questions.stem: In the hour before he came to the hospital, he had shaking chills and felt cold even though his temperature was already 38.9 °C (102.0 °F). Which of the following best explains the chills?
options: A raised hypothalamic set point above core temperature
Endotoxin-induced uncoupling of mitochondria in muscle
Loss of anterior hypothalamic heat-loss neurons
Cytokine-induced lowering of the hypothalamic set point
approach: Recall that pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) induce prostaglandin E2 in the preoptic hypothalamus.
PGE2 raises the temperature set point.
Until core temperature reaches the new set point, the body senses itself as too cold and conserves and makes heat by vasoconstriction and shivering.
questions.why: In infection, macrophages release IL-1, IL-6, and TNF. These cytokines induce COX-2 in the region of the preoptic hypothalamus, and the resulting PGE2 raises the thermoregulatory set point. While core temperature is still below the new set point, the hypothalamus triggers heat conservation and production: skin vasoconstriction, feeling cold, and shivering (chills). When the fever breaks and the set point falls, the opposite happens, with sweating and vasodilation. This is why fever is lowered by drugs that block prostaglandin synthesis.
whyNot: Correct.
Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation generates heat in brown fat and in malignant hyperthermia or salicylate toxicity. It does not cause the cold feeling and shivering of a rising fever.
Damage to the anterior hypothalamus impairs heat loss and causes hyperthermia, but it does not cause shivering in a feverish patient.
Cytokines raise the set point. A lowered set point would trigger sweating and vasodilation, as happens when a fever breaks.

case: A 10-day-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of 1 day of fever, poor feeding, and irritability. She was born at term by vaginal delivery. Her mother received no prenatal care. Her temperature is 38.7 °C (101.7 °F), pulse is 182/min, and respirations are 56/min. She is lethargic, and the anterior fontanelle is bulging. Lumbar puncture is performed. CSF analysis shows leukocytes 1,600/µL (N, 0 to 20/µL for age) with 85% neutrophils, glucose 15 mg/dL with a simultaneous blood glucose of 78 mg/dL (CSF to blood ratio normally above about 0.6), and protein 310 mg/dL (N, 20 to 150 mg/dL for age). Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in chains. Diagnosis: group B streptococcal meningitis.

questions.stem: Culture of the CSF grows the organism seen on Gram stain. Which of the following laboratory characteristics is this organism most likely to show?
options: Alpha hemolysis and optochin sensitivity
Beta hemolysis and bacitracin sensitivity
Beta hemolysis and bacitracin resistance
Gamma hemolysis and growth in 6.5% NaCl
approach: Gram-positive cocci in chains causing meningitis in a newborn point to Streptococcus agalactiae (group B).
Recall how streptococci are separated in the lab: hemolysis first, then bacitracin or optochin.
Group B streptococci are beta-hemolytic and bacitracin resistant, and they are CAMP test positive.
questions.why: Streptococcus agalactiae colonizes the vagina and rectum of many pregnant women and passes to the infant during delivery. It has a polysaccharide capsule that resists phagocytosis, which newborns handle poorly. In the lab it is beta-hemolytic, bacitracin resistant, CAMP test positive, and hydrolyzes hippurate. Screening pregnant women and giving intrapartum antibiotics prevents most early-onset disease. The other main neonatal meningitis pathogens are E. coli with the K1 capsule and Listeria monocytogenes, a gram-positive rod.
whyNot: Alpha hemolysis with optochin sensitivity identifies Streptococcus pneumoniae, which appears as lancet-shaped diplococci and causes meningitis in older children and adults.
Beta hemolysis with bacitracin sensitivity identifies Streptococcus pyogenes (group A), which causes pharyngitis and skin infections, not neonatal meningitis.
Correct.
Gamma hemolysis with growth in 6.5% salt identifies Enterococcus, which is an uncommon cause of neonatal meningitis.

questions.stem: The organisms that cause bacterial meningitis change with age. Which of the following organisms is a classic cause in both neonates and adults older than 60 years but is uncommon in healthy young adults?
options: Listeria monocytogenes
Haemophilus influenzae type b
Neisseria meningitidis
Escherichia coli K1
approach: List the causes by age: neonates (group B streptococcus, E. coli, Listeria), children and adults (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis), older adults (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, Listeria).
Find the organism on both the neonatal and older adult lists.
Listeria targets people with weak cell-mediated immunity: newborns, pregnant women, older adults, and the immunosuppressed.
questions.why: Listeria monocytogenes is a gram-positive rod with tumbling motility that lives inside cells and spreads from cell to cell using actin tails. Control depends on T cell-mediated immunity, which is immature in newborns and declines with age, pregnancy, and immunosuppression. It is acquired from unpasteurized dairy, soft cheese, and deli meats, and it grows at refrigerator temperature. That is why it appears on the neonatal list and again on the list for adults over about 60 years.
whyNot: Correct.
Haemophilus influenzae type b once caused much meningitis in children 6 months to 6 years old. The conjugate vaccine has made it rare, and it is not a typical cause in older adults.
N. meningitidis is a leading cause in adolescents and young adults, so it is not uncommon in that group.
E. coli K1 is a major cause of neonatal meningitis but is not a typical cause of community meningitis in older adults.

questions.stem: Her bulging fontanelle reflects raised intracranial pressure from cerebral edema. Which of the following processes most directly increases brain water in this condition?
options: Increased CSF secretion by the choroid plexus
Tearing of bridging veins with bleeding into the subdural space
Loss of astrocyte foot processes from viral lysis
Cytokine-mediated opening of endothelial tight junctions
approach: Recall that the blood-brain barrier depends on tight junctions between capillary endothelial cells, supported by astrocyte foot processes.
In bacterial meningitis, bacterial cell wall products activate microglia and macrophages, which release IL-1 and TNF.
These cytokines loosen endothelial tight junctions, so plasma fluid and protein leak into the brain (vasogenic edema).
questions.why: The blood-brain barrier is formed by endothelial tight junctions with a basement membrane and astrocyte foot processes. It also keeps antibodies and complement low in the CSF, which lets bacteria multiply once they arrive. In meningitis, bacterial products such as lipoteichoic acid and peptidoglycan activate microglia and macrophages through Toll-like receptors, and they release IL-1 and TNF. These cytokines activate the endothelium, bring in neutrophils, and open tight junctions, so fluid and protein leak into the brain. This vasogenic edema raises intracranial pressure, which in an infant with an open fontanelle makes the fontanelle bulge.
whyNot: The choroid plexus makes CSF at a fairly steady rate, and inflammation does not raise brain water by increasing its output.
Torn bridging veins cause a subdural hematoma after trauma or shaking. This adds a blood collection rather than water in brain tissue.
Her infection is bacterial. Direct viral lysis of astrocytes is not how bacterial meningitis damages the barrier.
Correct.

questions.stem: She recovers. At age 6 months, hearing testing shows bilateral hearing loss. The tympanic membranes look normal, and tympanometry shows normal middle ear pressure and movement. Which of the following is the most likely site of injury?
options: Ossicular chain of the middle ear
Cochlear hair cells of the inner ear
Eustachian tube draining the middle ear
Primary auditory cortex of the temporal lobes
approach: Normal eardrums and normal tympanometry rule out a conductive problem in the middle ear.
So the loss is sensorineural.
Bacterial meningitis spreads from the subarachnoid space to the inner ear and destroys cochlear hair cells.
questions.why: Sensorineural hearing loss is the most common lasting complication of bacterial meningitis. Bacteria and inflammation spread from the subarachnoid space into the cochlea through the cochlear aqueduct and internal acoustic canal, causing labyrinthitis that destroys hair cells and can later fill the cochlea with bone. Conductive loss comes from problems that block sound reaching the inner ear: cerumen, a perforated eardrum, middle ear fluid, eustachian tube dysfunction, otosclerosis, or cholesteatoma. Children who survive meningitis need prompt hearing testing.
whyNot: Ossicular damage causes conductive loss, as in cholesteatoma or otosclerosis. Middle ear movement on tympanometry would usually be abnormal.
Correct.
Eustachian tube dysfunction causes negative middle ear pressure or fluid and a conductive loss, which would show on tympanometry.
Bilateral cortical deafness is very rare and needs damage to both temporal lobes. Meningitis-related hearing loss comes from the cochlea.

dx: Herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis of the temporal lobe
case: A 36-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband because of 3 days of fever, headache, and increasingly strange behavior. She has complained of smelling burning rubber, and this morning she had a seizure that began with lip smacking. Her temperature is 38.8 °C (101.8 °F). She is disoriented and has difficulty naming objects. MRI of the brain shows T2 hyperintensity with small hemorrhages in the left medial temporal lobe and insula. CSF analysis shows leukocytes 180/µL (N, 0 to 5/µL), mostly lymphocytes; erythrocytes 400/µL (N, 0/µL); glucose 62 mg/dL (N, 40 to 70 mg/dL); and protein 95 mg/dL (N, 15 to 45 mg/dL). PCR of the CSF is positive for herpes simplex virus type 1 DNA. Diagnosis: HSV-1 encephalitis of the temporal lobe.

questions.stem: A 2-week-old boy born by vaginal delivery to a mother who had active genital vesicles at the time of birth develops lethargy and seizures. He was well during his first week. Which of the following herpesviruses is the most likely cause of his encephalitis?
options: Cytomegalovirus
Herpes simplex virus 2
Epstein-Barr virus
Varicella-zoster virus
approach: Note the timing and route: infection picked up during passage through a birth canal with active genital lesions.
Genital herpes is most often HSV-2, and neonatal HSV encephalitis appears in the first weeks of life.
Contrast congenital CMV, which crosses the placenta and is present at birth with periventricular calcifications.
questions.why: Each herpesvirus has its own CNS pattern. HSV-1 causes hemorrhagic encephalitis of the temporal lobes in adults, like this woman's. HSV-2 causes aseptic meningitis in adults and, when passed from the birth canal, neonatal encephalitis that appears in the first weeks of life. CMV causes congenital infection with periventricular calcifications and, in advanced AIDS, encephalitis and ventriculitis. EBV is linked to primary CNS lymphoma in AIDS.
whyNot: Congenital CMV is acquired across the placenta during pregnancy and shows at birth with periventricular calcifications, microcephaly, and hearing loss. It is not tied to genital vesicles at delivery.
Correct.
EBV causes infectious mononucleosis and is linked to primary CNS lymphoma in AIDS. It is not a cause of neonatal encephalitis from the birth canal.
Varicella-zoster virus causes chickenpox and shingles. Congenital varicella causes limb and skin scarring, and it is not linked to genital vesicles.

questions.stem: Before this illness, the virus that caused her encephalitis most likely persisted in a latent state in which of the following locations?
options: Memory B lymphocytes
Renal tubular epithelial cells
Sacral dorsal root ganglia
Trigeminal ganglion neurons
approach: HSV is an enveloped double-stranded DNA virus that establishes latency in sensory ganglion neurons.
HSV-1 usually infects the oral and facial region first, so it becomes latent in the trigeminal ganglion.
On reactivation it travels along axons, and in encephalitis it reaches the temporal and orbitofrontal lobes.
questions.why: Herpesviruses are enveloped double-stranded DNA viruses that remain for life after the first infection. HSV-1 enters sensory nerve endings in the mouth or face, travels up the axon to the trigeminal ganglion, and stays there as a quiet episome. Reactivation sends virus back down the axon to cause cold sores, and rarely the virus reaches the brain along trigeminal or olfactory pathways and causes temporal lobe encephalitis. JC polyomavirus is a different nervous system DNA virus: nonenveloped, latent in the kidney, and reactivated in immunosuppression.
whyNot: Memory B lymphocytes are the latent site of Epstein-Barr virus.
Renal tubular epithelium is the latent site of JC and BK polyomaviruses.
Sacral dorsal root ganglia are the usual latent site of HSV-2 after genital infection.
Correct.

topics: DNA viruses of the nervous system

questions.stem: During her seizure, temporal lobe neurons fire action potentials at very high rates. Which of the following sets the shortest possible interval between two action potentials in one of these neurons?
options: Inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels
Opening of delayed rectifier potassium channels
Activity of the sodium-potassium ATPase
Closure of potassium leak channels at rest
approach: The shortest interval between spikes is the absolute refractory period.
During this period no stimulus, however strong, can trigger a second spike.
This is because voltage-gated sodium channels are inactivated and cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes.
questions.why: An action potential starts when depolarization reaches threshold and voltage-gated sodium channels open. Within about a millisecond their inactivation gates close, and delayed potassium channels open to repolarize the membrane, often overshooting into an afterhyperpolarization. While the sodium channels are inactivated, no second action potential is possible (absolute refractory period). As they recover during repolarization, a stronger than normal stimulus can fire the cell (relative refractory period). The absolute refractory period sets the maximum firing rate.
whyNot: Correct.
Delayed potassium channels repolarize the membrane and cause the afterhyperpolarization, which underlies the relative refractory period. A strong stimulus can still fire the cell then.
The sodium-potassium ATPase maintains ion gradients over time but is not what limits the interval between individual spikes.
Potassium leak channels set the resting membrane potential. They do not cause the refractory period.

questions.stem: Two years later, she develops pain, redness, tearing, and photophobia of the right eye. Fluorescein staining shows a branching linear ulcer of the corneal epithelium with terminal bulbs. She does not wear contact lenses. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Acanthamoeba castellanii
Herpes simplex virus
Adenovirus
approach: A branching (dendritic) ulcer that stains with fluorescein is the hallmark of HSV keratitis.
HSV-1 latent in the trigeminal ganglion can reactivate along the ophthalmic division to the cornea.
No contact lens use makes Pseudomonas and Acanthamoeba less likely.
questions.why: Herpes simplex keratitis is usually reactivation of HSV-1 from the trigeminal ganglion along the ophthalmic nerve. It produces a dendritic ulcer of the corneal epithelium with terminal bulbs that stains with fluorescein. Repeated episodes can scar the stroma and are a major infectious cause of corneal blindness. Anterior uveitis (iritis) can also cause a painful red eye with photophobia, but it shows a ring of redness around the cornea (ciliary flush), a small irregular pupil, and cells in the anterior chamber, without an epithelial ulcer.
whyNot: Pseudomonas causes a rapidly spreading corneal ulcer with pus, mostly in contact lens wearers. It does not form a dendritic pattern.
Acanthamoeba keratitis occurs in contact lens wearers exposed to tap or pool water and causes severe pain with a ring-shaped stromal infiltrate.
Correct.
Adenovirus causes epidemic keratoconjunctivitis with a watery discharge, preauricular nodes, and subepithelial infiltrates, not a branching ulcer.

dx: West Nile virus encephalitis with acute flaccid paralysis
case: A 71-year-old man is brought to the emergency department in late August because of 4 days of fever, headache, and confusion and 1 day of weakness of his left leg. He lives in Colorado and spends his evenings gardening, and he recalls many mosquito bites. His temperature is 39.1 °C (102.4 °F). He is disoriented to place and time. The left leg has flaccid weakness with absent knee and ankle reflexes. Sensation is intact throughout. CSF analysis shows leukocytes 140/µL (N, 0 to 5/µL) with 70% lymphocytes, glucose 64 mg/dL (N, 40 to 70 mg/dL), and protein 110 mg/dL (N, 15 to 45 mg/dL). IgM antibody to West Nile virus is detected in the CSF. Diagnosis: West Nile virus encephalitis with acute flaccid paralysis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of humans in the transmission cycle of this virus?
options: Dead-end hosts with viremia too low to infect mosquitoes
Amplifying hosts whose viremia infects feeding mosquitoes
Reservoir hosts that maintain the virus between seasons
Primary hosts that spread virus by respiratory droplets
approach: Recall the West Nile cycle: Culex mosquitoes pass the virus among birds, which are the reservoir and amplifying hosts.
Infected mosquitoes sometimes bite humans or horses.
Human viremia is brief and low, so a mosquito biting a person rarely picks up enough virus to continue the cycle.
questions.why: West Nile virus and other arboviruses such as St. Louis encephalitis and eastern and western equine encephalitis viruses are maintained in a bird-mosquito-bird cycle. Birds develop high viremia and infect the Culex mosquitoes that feed on them. Humans and horses are incidental, dead-end hosts: their viremia is too low to infect mosquitoes. Most human infections cause no symptoms, and fewer than about 1 in 100 cause neuroinvasive disease, with older adults at highest risk of encephalitis and acute flaccid paralysis. Rare spread by transfusion or organ transplant still occurs.
whyNot: Correct.
Birds are the amplifying hosts. Human viremia is too low to infect mosquitoes.
Birds, with mosquitoes, maintain the virus in nature. Humans do not carry it between seasons.
West Nile virus is not spread between people by respiratory droplets. It reaches humans through mosquito bites.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the structure and genome of the virus causing his illness?
options: Nonenveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA
Enveloped, negative-sense single-stranded RNA
Enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA
Enveloped, double-stranded linear DNA
approach: Identify the virus: a mosquito-borne encephalitis with bird reservoirs in late summer is West Nile virus.
Classify it: West Nile is a flavivirus.
Flaviviruses are enveloped and have a positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome.
questions.why: West Nile virus is a flavivirus. It has a lipid envelope and a positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome that host ribosomes can translate directly. The envelope is easily damaged by drying and detergents, which fits its spread by mosquito bite rather than by contaminated surfaces. Compare the other nervous system RNA viruses: enteroviruses such as poliovirus are nonenveloped positive-sense picornaviruses spread by the fecal-oral route, and rabies is a bullet-shaped, enveloped, negative-sense rhabdovirus that travels up axons.
whyNot: This describes enteroviruses such as poliovirus, coxsackievirus, and echovirus. Being nonenveloped lets them survive the gut and spread by the fecal-oral route.
This describes rabies virus, a rhabdovirus carried by bites from bats, raccoons, and dogs.
Correct.
This describes herpesviruses, such as HSV, which become latent in sensory ganglia.

topics: RNA viruses of the nervous system

questions.stem: His leg weakness resembles that of paralytic poliomyelitis. In both conditions, the virus damages which of the following structures?
options: Dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons
Anterior horn motor neurons
Lateral corticospinal tract axons
Motor end plates at the neuromuscular junction
approach: Sort the signs: flaccid weakness with absent reflexes is a lower motor neuron pattern, and sensation is intact.
Asymmetric, purely motor lower motor neuron weakness with fever points to the cell bodies of motor neurons.
These cell bodies lie in the anterior (ventral) horn of the spinal cord gray matter.
questions.why: Poliovirus is a fecal-oral enterovirus that multiplies in the gut and lymphoid tissue, then in a small fraction of people reaches the spinal cord and destroys anterior horn motor neurons. West Nile virus can attack the same neurons. Loss of the lower motor neuron causes asymmetric flaccid paralysis, absent reflexes, fasciculations, and later atrophy, with sensation spared because sensory neurons are not involved. Decades after polio, survivors can develop new weakness and fatigue (post-polio syndrome) as the remaining enlarged motor units fail.
whyNot: Damage to dorsal root ganglia would cause sensory loss and sensory ataxia. His sensation is intact.
Correct.
Lateral corticospinal tract damage is an upper motor neuron lesion with spasticity, hyperreflexia, and a Babinski sign, not flaccid weakness with absent reflexes.
Disorders of the neuromuscular junction, such as botulism or myasthenia gravis, cause symmetric or fluctuating weakness that often begins in cranial muscles. His weakness is limited to one leg.

topics: Upper versus lower motor neuron signs

questions.stem: He dies 2 weeks later. Microscopic examination of his brainstem and spinal cord is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Neutrophilic exudate filling the subarachnoid space
Spongiform vacuoles in neuropil without inflammation
Eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in Purkinje cells
Perivascular lymphocytic cuffs and microglial nodules
approach: His CSF shows lymphocytes with normal glucose, which points to viral rather than bacterial infection.
Recall the general tissue pattern of viral encephalitis.
It includes lymphocytes around blood vessels, clusters of microglia, and microglia engulfing dying neurons (neuronophagia).
questions.why: Most viral encephalitides share a common tissue pattern. Lymphocytes and macrophages gather around small vessels (perivascular cuffs), microglia form small clusters called microglial nodules, and microglia engulf infected dying neurons (neuronophagia). Some viruses add a specific clue: HSV causes hemorrhagic necrosis of the temporal lobes, and rabies causes Negri bodies, eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in hippocampal and Purkinje neurons. Rabies is acquired from bat, raccoon, or dog bites and causes agitation and hydrophobia.
whyNot: A neutrophilic exudate in the subarachnoid space marks bacterial meningitis, with low CSF glucose.
Spongiform change without inflammation marks prion disease, such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
Negri bodies in Purkinje and hippocampal neurons mark rabies, which has a different history: an animal bite, agitation, and hydrophobia.
Correct.

case: A 4-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of 5 days of constipation followed by 2 days of poor feeding, a weak cry, and decreased movement. He was previously healthy and developing normally. His temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F). He has bilateral ptosis, dilated pupils that react sluggishly to light, a weak suck and gag, and generalized hypotonia with poor head control. Deep tendon reflexes are decreased. He follows faces with his eyes and responds to touch on all four limbs. Botulinum toxin is detected in his stool. Diagnosis: infant botulism.

questions.stem: Stool culture also grows Clostridium botulinum. Which of the following best explains how this infant acquired the disease, in contrast with the usual adult foodborne form?
options: Ingestion of preformed toxin in home-canned food
Spores germinating in a contaminated skin wound
Inhalation of toxin in contaminated household dust
Spores germinating in the colon and making toxin
approach: Note that both the organism and its toxin are in the stool, so the bacteria are living in his gut.
Young infants lack the mature gut flora that normally keeps spores from germinating.
Swallowed spores, from honey or soil dust, germinate in the colon and make toxin there.
questions.why: Botulism has three main forms with the same toxin and the same neurologic picture. In foodborne botulism, adults eat preformed toxin in improperly canned or preserved food. In infant botulism, babies under 1 year swallow spores from honey or environmental dust, and the spores germinate and colonize the immature colon, producing toxin in place. Constipation is often the first sign. In wound botulism, spores germinate in a contaminated wound, often from injection drug use. All forms cause descending symmetric flaccid paralysis that starts with cranial nerves, without fever or sensory loss.
whyNot: Preformed toxin in food causes adult foodborne botulism. Organisms do not need to grow in the gut, and constipation is not the first sign.
Spores growing in a wound cause wound botulism, typically in people who inject drugs. He has no wound.
Spores, not toxin, are carried in household dust. Inhaled toxin is a bioterrorism concern and would not explain the organism growing in his stool.
Correct.

questions.stem: Electromyography shows small compound muscle action potentials that increase in amplitude during rapid repetitive nerve stimulation at 50 Hz. Which of the following best explains this increase?
options: Saturation of acetylcholinesterase prolonging ACh action
Presynaptic calcium buildup increasing vesicle release
Recovery of postsynaptic receptors from desensitization
Removal of bound toxin from terminals by nerve activity
approach: Recall the steps of transmission: an action potential opens presynaptic calcium channels, calcium triggers SNARE-mediated vesicle fusion, and ACh acts on nicotinic receptors.
Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins, so fewer vesicles are released and the muscle response is small.
With rapid stimulation, calcium builds up in the terminal and raises the chance of release from the remaining working machinery.
questions.why: At the neuromuscular junction, an action potential opens voltage-gated calcium channels in the nerve terminal. Calcium triggers SNARE proteins to fuse vesicles with the membrane and release acetylcholine, which opens nicotinic receptors on the muscle. Acetylcholinesterase ends the signal. Botulinum toxin is a protease that cleaves SNARE proteins, so less ACh is released and the baseline response is small. During rapid stimulation, calcium accumulates in the terminal and increases release, so the response grows. Lambert-Eaton syndrome shows the same increment for a related reason, while myasthenia gravis shows a decrement with slow repetitive stimulation because of fewer postsynaptic receptors.
whyNot: Acetylcholinesterase is not saturated at a normal junction, and the toxin's problem is too little ACh release, not faster breakdown.
Correct.
The primary defect is presynaptic. Receptor desensitization would reduce, not increase, the response during rapid stimulation.
Botulinum toxin is internalized and its cleavage of SNARE proteins is not reversed by nerve activity. Recovery takes weeks to months while terminals sprout and SNAREs are replaced.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman has drooping eyelids and double vision that worsen toward evening. Her serum contains antibodies to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, and CT scan of the chest shows an anterior mediastinal mass. Which of the following immune mechanisms most directly causes her weakness?
options: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation at the end plate
Immune complex deposition in muscle capillaries
IgG binding to a fixed cell surface antigen
T cell-mediated injury of the motor nerve terminal
approach: Identify the disease: fatiguable ptosis and diplopia with acetylcholine receptor antibodies and a thymic mass is myasthenia gravis.
Ask what the antibody targets: a receptor fixed on the muscle cell surface.
Antibody against a cell surface or matrix antigen is type II hypersensitivity.
questions.why: In myasthenia gravis, IgG antibodies bind nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. They block the receptor, cross-link receptors so they are taken into the cell and destroyed, and activate complement that damages the end plate. This is type II hypersensitivity. It is associated with thymic hyperplasia and thymoma. Lambert-Eaton syndrome is also type II, with antibodies to presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, often with small cell lung cancer. Multiple sclerosis and ADEM are T cell-mediated. Botulism, in contrast, is caused by a bacterial toxin and involves no immune attack.
whyNot: IgE-mediated mast cell release is type I hypersensitivity, as in anaphylaxis and asthma. It does not cause fatiguable weakness.
Immune complex deposition is type III hypersensitivity, as in serum sickness and lupus nephritis. In myasthenia gravis the antibody binds a fixed tissue antigen.
Correct.
T cell-mediated injury is type IV hypersensitivity, as in multiple sclerosis. Myasthenia gravis is caused by antibodies against a postsynaptic receptor.

questions.stem: The infant's dilated, sluggish pupils result from blocked acetylcholine release by postganglionic parasympathetic neurons. In which of the following ganglia are the cell bodies of these neurons located?
options: Ciliary ganglion
Otic ganglion
Pterygopalatine ganglion
Superior cervical ganglion
approach: The muscle that constricts the pupil is the sphincter pupillae, supplied by parasympathetic fibers.
Preganglionic fibers come from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus and travel with CN III.
They synapse in the ciliary ganglion, whose postganglionic fibers reach the eye in the short ciliary nerves.
questions.why: The four parasympathetic ganglia of the head each serve specific targets. The ciliary ganglion (CN III) supplies the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle. The pterygopalatine ganglion (CN VII) supplies the lacrimal gland and nasal glands. The submandibular ganglion (CN VII) supplies the submandibular and sublingual glands. The otic ganglion (CN IX) supplies the parotid. Botulinum toxin blocks ACh release at all cholinergic terminals, including these autonomic fibers, so it causes dilated pupils, dry mouth, and constipation as well as weakness.
whyNot: Correct.
The otic ganglion relays CN IX fibers to the parotid gland. Blocking it causes dry mouth, not pupil changes.
The pterygopalatine ganglion relays CN VII fibers to the lacrimal gland and nasal mucosa.
The superior cervical ganglion is sympathetic. It supplies the pupillary dilator, and its loss causes a small pupil, as in Horner syndrome.

dx: Generalized tetanus after a puncture wound
case: A 62-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of 2 days of jaw stiffness and difficulty swallowing, followed by painful spasms of her neck and back muscles. Ten days ago she stepped on a nail while gardening and cleaned the wound herself. Her last tetanus immunization was in childhood. Her temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 148/88 mm Hg. She is alert and oriented. She cannot open her mouth more than 1 cm, and her face shows a fixed grin with raised eyebrows. A loud noise triggers a spasm that arches her back. Sensation is normal. A healing puncture wound is present on the sole of the right foot. Diagnosis: generalized tetanus.

questions.stem: After recovery, she is given tetanus toxoid. Which of the following best describes how this vaccine prevents disease?
options: Antibodies against the bacterium block spore germination
Live attenuated bacteria induce intestinal IgA
IgG neutralizes toxin before it binds nerve terminals
Transferred antitoxin gives lasting passive immunity
approach: A toxoid is a toxin made harmless, usually with formaldehyde, that keeps its antigenic shape.
It induces active immunity: IgG and memory B cells against tetanospasmin.
Circulating IgG binds toxin released in a wound before it can enter nerve endings.
questions.why: Tetanus is caused entirely by tetanospasmin, made by Clostridium tetani after spores enter a deep or dirty wound, or the umbilical stump in newborns. The toxoid vaccine induces IgG antitoxin, which neutralizes the toxin in the blood and tissues before it binds and enters motor nerve terminals. Once inside neurons, toxin is out of reach of antibody. Recovering from tetanus does not make a person immune, because the amount of toxin that causes disease is too small to stimulate antibodies, so she still needs the vaccine. Boosters are given about every 10 years, and vaccinating pregnant women protects newborns because IgG crosses the placenta.
whyNot: The toxoid targets the toxin, not the bacterium, and spore germination in a wound is not prevented by vaccination.
Tetanus toxoid is an inactivated toxin given by injection. It is not a live vaccine, and gut IgA plays no part in protection.
Correct.
Passive immunity comes from tetanus immune globulin, given for wounds in poorly immunized people. It lasts only weeks. The toxoid produces active, long-lasting immunity.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the action of the toxin responsible for her spasms?
options: Blocks glycine and GABA release from spinal interneurons
Blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
Binds and activates nicotinic receptors on muscle
Inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the motor end plate
approach: Her paralysis is spastic: sustained contraction and spasms, not weakness.
Spastic paralysis from a toxin means loss of inhibition of motor neurons.
Tetanospasmin travels retrogradely up motor axons to the spinal cord and blocks release of inhibitory transmitters from interneurons.
questions.why: Tetanospasmin enters motor nerve terminals near the wound and travels up the axon by retrograde transport to the spinal cord and brainstem. It then crosses into inhibitory interneurons, including Renshaw cells, and cleaves the SNARE protein synaptobrevin, so these cells cannot release glycine and GABA. Motor neurons lose their inhibition and fire uncontrollably, causing trismus, risus sardonicus, opisthotonus, and spasms. Botulinum toxin uses the same type of SNARE cleavage but stays at the neuromuscular junction, so it blocks ACh release and causes flaccid paralysis.
whyNot: Correct.
Blocking ACh release at the neuromuscular junction is the action of botulinum toxin, which causes flaccid, not spastic, paralysis.
Sustained activation of muscle nicotinic receptors causes brief fasciculations and then a depolarizing block with flaccid weakness. Tetanospasmin does not act on muscle receptors.
Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, such as organophosphates, cause cholinergic excess with salivation, miosis, and muscle twitching followed by weakness. They are not bacterial toxins.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her alpha motor neurons now fire in prolonged bursts after a sensory stimulus such as a loud noise?
options: Action potential amplitude grows with stimulus strength
Graded potentials spread along the axon without decay
The motor neuron refractory period becomes shorter
EPSPs summate at the axon hillock without IPSPs
approach: A motor neuron fires when the sum of its synaptic inputs depolarizes the axon hillock to threshold.
Excitatory inputs give EPSPs, and inhibitory interneurons normally give IPSPs that offset them.
With inhibition removed by the toxin, EPSPs from a stimulus summate unopposed and drive repeated firing.
questions.why: EPSPs and IPSPs are graded potentials. Their size varies with input, they fade with distance, and they add together in time (temporal summation) and across many synapses (spatial summation). The axon hillock has the highest density of sodium channels and the lowest threshold, so the net sum there decides whether an action potential fires. Glycine and GABA from inhibitory interneurons open chloride channels and create IPSPs. When tetanospasmin removes them, any excitatory input, such as a startle from a loud noise, pushes many motor neurons to threshold at once and keeps them firing.
whyNot: Action potentials are all-or-none. A stronger stimulus raises firing frequency, not the size of each spike.
Graded potentials decay with distance. Only action potentials travel along the axon without losing size.
The refractory period depends on sodium channel inactivation and does not change in tetanus. The problem is loss of inhibitory input.
Correct.

questions.stem: On the fifth hospital day, she has profuse sweating, a pulse of 140/min, and blood pressure that swings between 190/110 and 90/50 mm Hg. This is attributed to loss of inhibition of sympathetic preganglionic neurons. In which of the following locations are the cell bodies of these neurons found?
options: Paravertebral chain ganglia from T1 to L2
Lateral horn of spinal segments T1 to L2
Gray matter of sacral spinal segments S2 to S4
Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
approach: Recall that the sympathetic system has thoracolumbar outflow and the parasympathetic system has craniosacral outflow.
Sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies sit in the intermediolateral cell column, which forms the lateral horn of spinal segments T1 to L2.
Their axons leave through ventral roots and white rami to synapse in chain or prevertebral ganglia, where the postganglionic cell bodies lie.
questions.why: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons lie in the lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column) of the spinal cord from T1 to L2. Their short axons synapse in paravertebral chain ganglia or prevertebral ganglia near the aorta, and long postganglionic axons reach the target organs. Parasympathetic preganglionic neurons lie in brainstem nuclei of CN III, VII, IX, and X and in sacral segments S2 to S4, with long preganglionic axons that synapse in ganglia near or in the target organ. In tetanus, toxin removes inhibition of the sympathetic neurons too, causing autonomic storms that are a major cause of death.
whyNot: Paravertebral chain ganglia contain the sympathetic postganglionic cell bodies, not the preganglionic ones.
Correct.
Sacral segments S2 to S4 hold parasympathetic preganglionic neurons that supply the bladder, rectum, and genitals.
The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus holds parasympathetic preganglionic neurons for the thoracic and abdominal organs. Vagal activity slows the heart.

dx: Cryptococcal meningitis in advanced HIV infection
case: A 34-year-old man with HIV infection who stopped antiretroviral therapy 2 years ago comes to the emergency department because of 3 weeks of worsening headache, fever, and nausea and 2 days of confusion. His temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F). He is drowsy and has mild neck stiffness and bilateral papilledema. His CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 36/mm3 (N, 500 to 1,500/mm3). Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 38 cm H2O (N, 10 to 20 cm H2O). CSF analysis shows leukocytes 22/µL (N, 0 to 5/µL), mostly lymphocytes; glucose 30 mg/dL (N, 40 to 70 mg/dL); and protein 85 mg/dL (N, 15 to 45 mg/dL). CSF cryptococcal antigen is positive. Diagnosis: cryptococcal meningitis in advanced HIV infection.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely to be seen on microscopic examination of his CSF?
options: Broad nonseptate hyphae with right-angle branching
Budding yeasts surrounded by wide clear halos
Spherules filled with endospores
Narrow septate hyphae with acute-angle branching
approach: A positive cryptococcal antigen identifies Cryptococcus neoformans.
Cryptococcus is a yeast with a thick polysaccharide capsule, and the antigen test detects that capsule.
India ink outlines the capsule as a clear halo around budding yeast cells.
questions.why: Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated yeast found in soil contaminated with pigeon droppings. It is inhaled, and in people with very low CD4 counts it spreads to the meninges. Its polysaccharide capsule blocks phagocytosis and is the antigen measured in CSF and serum. On India ink, the capsule excludes the ink and appears as a clear halo around round budding yeasts. Mucicarmine stains the capsule red in tissue.
whyNot: Broad nonseptate hyphae branching at right angles are Mucor and Rhizopus, which invade the sinuses, orbit, and brain in diabetic ketoacidosis.
Correct.
Spherules full of endospores are Coccidioides, from soil in the southwestern United States, which can cause chronic basilar meningitis.
Narrow septate hyphae with acute-angle branching are Aspergillus, which causes invasive lung disease in neutropenia.

questions.stem: Which of the following most likely explains his markedly increased CSF opening pressure?
options: Increased CSF production by inflamed choroid plexus
Obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct by a granuloma
Vasogenic edema from a ring-enhancing brain abscess
Yeast and capsule blocking arachnoid granulations
approach: Recall that CSF is made by the choroid plexus and absorbed into venous sinuses through arachnoid granulations.
In cryptococcal meningitis, large numbers of yeasts and shed capsular polysaccharide fill the subarachnoid space.
They clog the arachnoid granulations, so CSF outflow falls and pressure rises, often with normal-sized ventricles.
questions.why: Raised opening pressure is common and dangerous in cryptococcal meningitis in AIDS. Yeasts and capsular polysaccharide accumulate in the subarachnoid space and block CSF absorption through the arachnoid granulations. Pressure rises even though inflammation is mild, because a CD4 count this low allows little immune response. High pressure causes headache, papilledema, vision loss, cranial nerve palsies, and death, so it is relieved with repeated lumbar punctures. The other key fungal CNS infection to know is rhinocerebral mucormycosis in diabetic ketoacidosis, with a black necrotic nasal or palatal eschar that spreads to the orbit and brain.
whyNot: The choroid plexus does not increase CSF output enough to explain this. The problem is reduced absorption.

Aqueduct obstruction causes noncommunicating hydrocephalus with enlarged lateral and third ventricles. Cryptococcal meningitis raises pressure through diffusely blocked absorption, often with normal-sized ventricles.
A ring-enhancing abscess would show as a focal mass on imaging, as with toxoplasmosis. His findings fit diffuse meningitis.
Correct.

questions.stem: He again declines antiretroviral therapy after treatment. Four months later, he has a focal seizure followed by right-sided weakness. He has lived his whole life in Ohio and keeps two outdoor cats. MRI of the brain shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema in the basal ganglia and at the gray-white junction. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Toxoplasma gondii
Taenia solium
Naegleria fowleri
Plasmodium falciparum
approach: Note the setting: AIDS with a CD4 count below 100/mm3.
Multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia in this setting are most often toxoplasmosis, from reactivation of tissue cysts.
Check the other parasites against the history: no travel, no freshwater exposure, and lesions that do not fit them.
questions.why: Toxoplasma gondii is acquired from oocysts in cat feces or tissue cysts in undercooked meat, and it stays latent in brain and muscle for life. When the CD4 count falls below about 100/mm3, cysts reactivate and form multiple ring-enhancing abscesses, often in the basal ganglia and at the gray-white junction, causing seizures and focal deficits. Primary CNS lymphoma is the main alternative and is often a single lesion. Neurocysticercosis comes from swallowing Taenia solium eggs shed by a human tapeworm carrier, and Naegleria fowleri enters through the cribriform plate after swimming in warm fresh water.
whyNot: Correct.

Neurocysticercosis causes brain cysts and seizures after swallowing T. solium eggs, usually in people from or exposed to endemic areas. It is not tied to AIDS, and cysts often show a scolex or calcify.
Naegleria fowleri causes a rapidly fatal meningoencephalitis within days of swimming in warm fresh water. It does not cause ring-enhancing lesions.
Cerebral malaria follows travel to an endemic area and causes coma from sequestered parasitized red cells, not ring-enhancing lesions.

questions.stem: Two years later, still untreated, he develops aphasia, right arm weakness, and visual field loss that progress over 6 weeks. He is afebrile. MRI shows multiple asymmetric nonenhancing lesions of the subcortical white matter without mass effect. Which of the following is most likely to be seen in a brain biopsy specimen?
options: Multinucleated giant cells with microglial nodules
Necrotic foci containing tachyzoites and cysts
Oligodendrocytes with enlarged glassy nuclei
Atypical B cells cuffing blood vessels
approach: Note the setting of severe immunosuppression and the course over weeks.
Multifocal nonenhancing white matter lesions without mass effect suggest progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML).
PML is JC virus infection that kills oligodendrocytes, whose nuclei swell with viral inclusions.
questions.why: Most adults carry JC polyomavirus latently in the kidney. In severe immunosuppression, such as AIDS with a very low CD4 count or treatment with natalizumab or rituximab, the virus reactivates and infects oligodendrocytes. It lyses them, causing patchy demyelination that grows and merges in the subcortical white matter. Infected oligodendrocytes have enlarged nuclei with glassy viral inclusions, and astrocytes become large and bizarre. Patients develop rapidly progressive focal deficits, and the lesions typically do not enhance or cause mass effect.
whyNot: Multinucleated giant cells and microglial nodules mark HIV encephalitis, which causes slowly progressive dementia with diffuse, symmetric white matter changes rather than focal deficits.
Necrotic foci with tachyzoites and cysts mark toxoplasmosis, which forms ring-enhancing lesions with edema.
Correct.
Atypical B cells around vessels mark primary CNS lymphoma, which enhances and usually causes mass effect.
